1.meaning: "By the fig!" Allah opens the surah with a solemn oath, swearing by the fig — the well-known sweet fruit, and by extension the blessed lands (such as the region of Jerusalem) where fig trees flourish and where prophets were sent. In Arabic, swearing by a created thing signals its importance and calls the listener to pay close attention to what the oath will affirm.
1.grammar: The opening wa- here is the "waw of oath" — it means "by" and turns the phrase into a solemn vow ("By the fig!"), not the ordinary "and." Attached to it is the definite article al- ("the"). Because tā is a "sun letter," the lām of al- assimilates into it in pronunciation: the cluster is read at-tīn, and that assimilation is exactly what the shadda (doubling) on تِّ marks — so the written tāʾ carries the trace of the swallowed lām (full word: wal-tīni). The final -i ending is genitive (the jarr case), which is required because any noun governed by the oath-waw must take the genitive; so the -i is the grammatical fingerprint that this noun is the thing being sworn by.

2.meaning: "And by the olive!" The oath continues, now swearing by the olive — its fruit and its prized oil, and by extension the blessed lands where the olive grows (associated with Jerusalem and the Holy Land). Pairing the fig and the olive evokes both nourishment and a place steeped in prophetic history.
2.grammar: Here the wa- is the connecting "and," linking this second sworn-by noun to the first ("the fig and the olive") and carrying the force of the oath across to the olive as well. It too takes the definite article al-. As with the fig, zāy is a "sun letter," so the lām of al- assimilates into it: the lām is not pronounced separately, and the only orthographic sign of this is the shadda (doubling) on the zāy (زَّ). The word is read wal-zaytūni — the genitive -i ending again matching تِّينِ before it, because it is likewise an object of the oath (the jarr case governed by the oath-waw).

1.meaning: "And by the Mount" — an oath sworn upon a great mountain. The word ṭūr means a mountain (here the mountain of Sinai where Allah spoke directly to the Prophet Musa). The opening "and" carries the force of a solemn oath: Allah swears by this sacred site to lend weight to the truth that follows.
1.grammar: The prefix wa- here is the "oath particle": placed before a noun it means "by…" and is used to swear by something sacred. Because of this oath particle, the noun is in the genitive case, which is why it ends in -i (ṭūri rather than ṭūru). So the -i ending is the grammatical sign that this word is the thing being sworn by. This word is also the first term (mudhaf) of a construct phrase with the next word — "the Mount of Sinai."
1.root: ط-و-ر (ṭ-w-r) — a mountain; by extension a boundary, stage or limit

2.meaning: "Sinai" — the proper name of the specific mountain just mentioned, identifying it as the Mount of Sinai (also rendered Sīnīn), the hallowed place where Allah addressed the Prophet Musa. It pins down exactly which mountain the oath intends.
2.grammar: This proper place-name is the second term (mudhaf ilayh) of a construct phrase (iḍāfa) with the preceding word: ṭūri sīnīna = "the Mount of Sinai." The second term of such a construct must be genitive, so sīnīna is in the genitive case. Normally the genitive ending is -i, but foreign and certain proper names are "diptotes" (they refuse the -i ending) and take -a instead. So the final -a here is functioning as a genitive marker — the special ending such names use — not as an accusative.

1.meaning: "And this" — the opening wāw is the oath particle ("and" used to mean "I swear by"), continuing the series of oaths from the previous two verses. "This" is a near-demonstrative pointing to something present and known — here the city of Makkah, pointed to as if right before the eyes.
1.grammar: The wāw here is the wāw of oath (qasam), so "and" really carries the force of "and I swear by." هٰذَا is a demonstrative pronoun, masculine singular, used for something near ("this" rather than "that"). As a demonstrative it is indeclinable (mabnī) — its form never changes for case — but in this oath it occupies the position of the genitive (the thing sworn by). The noun that follows, "the city," is not a forward reference; it stands in apposition to هٰذَا (a badal) and simply spells out what "this" refers to: "this [city]."

2.meaning: The city — a settled town or inhabited place. In context it is Makkah specifically, the sacred city; the definite article "al-" ("the") marks it as a particular, well-known city rather than just any town.
2.grammar: الۡ is the definite article "the." The noun is masculine singular. The final -i (kasra) ending is genitive case. The case governor is the oath wāw itself, which functions like a preposition and puts what is sworn by into the genitive. That word is the demonstrative هٰذَا, but because هٰذَا is indeclinable it cannot show the ending; بَلَد, standing in apposition to it (a badal), carries the genitive inflection on its behalf. So the -i marks بَلَد as part of the thing being sworn by: "by this city."

3.meaning: Trustworthy / faithful / reliable — and so, of a place, secure and inviolable. The faʿīl form أَمِين describes the city as one that can be relied upon: a sanctuary in which people and life are safe and violence is forbidden. (The plainer word for "safe" as a state is آمِن, the active participle; أَمِين stresses the trustworthy, dependable quality, which is why it is also used of a person who can be trusted.)
3.grammar: الۡ is the definite article "the," repeated because this adjective describes a definite noun (Arabic adjectives match their noun in definiteness). اَمِيۡن is an adjective on the faʿīl pattern, masculine singular, meaning "trustworthy, reliable" (distinct from the active participle آمِن, "safe"). Its final -i (kasra) ending is genitive, matching بَلَد ("city") — adjectives agree with the noun they describe in case, so since "city" is genitive, this adjective is too: "the trustworthy city."

1.meaning: An emphatic opener meaning roughly 'most certainly' or 'indeed, in truth'. It is not a single word but a fusion of two particles that together swear to and stress what follows, assuring the listener that the coming statement is an established fact.

parts.en: certainly / already (with a past verb, confirms the act really happened)

1.grammar: Two particles joined: the la- is the 'lam of emphasis', adding the force of an oath ('We truly...'); qad before a past-tense verb confirms the action is real and completed. Together they make the next verb a solemn, certain declaration. Neither part changes for case or person; they simply intensify.

2.meaning: 'We created / We brought into being from nothing'. The royal 'We' here is the majestic plural used of Allah, signalling greatness and power, not number. It points to an act of origination that is finished and beyond doubt.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb. The attached -nā ending is the subject 'we', so the doer is built right into the word ('We created'). Being past tense, it states a completed act. Used of Allah, this 'We' is the plural of majesty, expressing grandeur rather than plurality.

3.meaning: 'The human being / humankind' — the species man, considered as Allah's creation. The definite article 'the' generalises it, so it speaks of human beings as a kind, not one particular person.
3.grammar: A noun with the prefix al- ('the'). The final -a (insāna) is the accusative ending, which marks it as the direct object — the one being acted upon: 'We created the human'. The 'the' here generalises, covering humankind as a whole.
3.root: ا-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — to be sociable, familiar, humane (the human as a social, familiar being)

4.meaning: 'In / within'. A small linking word (preposition) that places the human inside or in the state of what follows — here, fashioned 'in' the best form.
4.grammar: A preposition meaning 'in'. It governs the noun after it, putting that noun into the genitive case. It sets up the phrase 'in the best...', describing the state or mould in which the human was made. The long final -ī is part of the word itself, not a case ending.

5.meaning: 'Best / finest / most beautiful'. A superlative describing the form of the human as the very highest, most excellent of its kind — none more well-made.
5.grammar: A superlative on the pattern afʿal ('most ...'), so 'best' or 'finest'. Its final -i (aḥsani) is the genitive ending, caused by the preposition fī before it ('in the best...'). It is the first part (the muḍāf) of a possessive pairing with the next word: 'the best OF moulds'.
5.root: ح-س-ن (ḥ-s-n) — to be good, beautiful, excellent

6.meaning: 'Form / mould / proportioned stature'. The word denotes a thing set straight and shaped in right, balanced proportion — the upright, well-ordered design and constitution in which the human being was fashioned. The phrase 'best of moulds' praises both the body's symmetry and the inner faculties given to man.

parts.en: shaping into right proportion / a moulding, stature

6.grammar: A verbal noun (masdar) of Form II (verb qawwama, masdar pattern tafʿīl), which carries the sense of 'making something straight and well-proportioned' — hence a 'moulding' or 'shaping'. Its final -in (taqwīmin) is the genitive ending with nunation (the -n sound) marking it as indefinite ('a mould'); the genitive is required because it is the second, possessed part (the muḍāf ilayh) of the pairing 'best of [a] mould'.
6.root: ق-و-م (q-w-m) — to stand, rise, be upright, set straight

1.meaning: A connecting particle meaning 'then' or 'afterward.' Unlike a simple 'and,' it signals a sequence with a gap — something that comes later, after an interval, marking a turn from what was just said (man's noble creation) to a contrasting next stage.
1.grammar: An indeclinable particle of sequence — it has no case ending and never changes form. It joins two statements while signaling that the second follows the first after a delay or with a sense of progression, here pivoting to the contrast that follows.

2.meaning: 'We sent him back' or 'We reduced/returned him.' Allah speaks of bringing the human being down to a lowered state — whether the decline of feeble old age or, by other interpretations, the abasement of the Fire for those who reject faith.
2.grammar: A past-tense verb. The attached -nā is the subject 'we' (the majestic 'We' of Allah), telling who did the action; the final -hu is the object 'him,' the one acted upon. So the piece literally reads 'we-returned-him.' The root ر-د-د already has two identical final letters (a geminate root). When a suffix that begins with a consonant is added — here -nā — those two dāls are written out separately, the first carrying a sukun (radad-nā). The doubling belongs to the root itself; attaching the pronoun is simply the condition under which the two letters appear spelled apart rather than merged.
2.root: ر-د-د (r-d-d) — to return, send back, turn away

3.meaning: '(To the) lowest' — the very bottom, the most abased and degraded point. It names the depth to which the person is brought down.
3.grammar: A superlative adjective ('most low / lowest') on the pattern afʿal. Here it functions adverbially, as an accusative of place answering 'to where?' — 'to the lowest' — which is why it carries the accusative ending -a. The fatḥa on the final letter is simply that accusative marker for this adverbial use.
3.root: س-ف-ل (s-f-l) — to be low, sink, be at the bottom

4.meaning: 'Of the low ones' — those who are sunken, base, or fallen low. Paired with the previous word it forms the sweeping phrase 'the lowest of the low.'
4.grammar: An active participle ('one who is low') made plural. The -īna ending is the masculine sound plural in the genitive/accusative form; here it works as a genitive 'of the low ones,' so the whole reads 'the lowest OF the low.' The long ā after the first letter marks it as a participle — the doer/holder of the quality.
4.root: س-ف-ل (s-f-l) — to be low, sink, be at the bottom

1.meaning: An exceptive particle meaning 'except' or 'save for.' It carves out an exception from the gloomy statement just before (that man is reduced 'to the lowest of the low'), signalling that one group is exempted from that fate.
1.grammar: A particle of exception (it has no case ending of its own). It works on what came before: the previous verse said man is brought low, and 'illā' introduces the people who are the exception to that. It governs the noun-phrase that follows ('those who believe…').

2.meaning: 'Those who' — a relative pronoun pointing to a defined group of people whose description follows in the next words (namely, the ones who believe and do good).
2.grammar: A masculine plural relative pronoun ('the ones who…'). Its form is fixed and does not change for case, but here it stands as the exception governed by 'illā.' The '-īna' shape marks it as plural and masculine, so it covers a whole community, not one person. A relative clause must follow to complete the sense, which it does with 'āmanū.'

3.meaning: 'They believed' — they came to genuine faith: trusting and affirming Allah, His messengers, and the truth. The root carries the ideas of security and trust, so to believe is to place one's heart in safe trust.
3.grammar: A past-tense verb; the base 3rd-person-masculine-singular form is 'āmana' ('he believed'), and the '-ū' ending makes it the 'they' subject for a group of males (or a mixed group): 'they believed.' This is Form IV, whose defining shape is 'afʿala' (a prefixed hamza + short 'a' on the first root letter), which often makes a root transitive or causative — here it gives the settled sense 'to come to / hold faith.' (The long 'ā-' you see at the start of 'āmana' is not the marker of Form IV; it is simply two hamzas merging — the Form IV prefix-hamza plus the root's own hamza, أَ + ء → آ — a contraction specific to this hamzated root.) Being past tense, it presents their faith as an established fact.

4.meaning: 'And they did / and they worked' — and they put faith into action through deeds. The word for 'do' here specifically means purposeful work and conduct, not idle activity.
4.grammar: The 'wa-' prefix simply means 'and,' joining this verb to 'believed.' The stem is a Form I past-tense verb whose base 3rd-person-masculine-singular form is 'ʿamila' ('he did, he worked'), and the '-ū' ending again marks 'they' (a group): 'they did.' So faith ('āmanū') and action ('ʿamilū') are paired as two things the same people do.
4.root: ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) — to do, to work, deeds

5.meaning: 'The righteous deeds' — good, wholesome, upright actions; works that are sound and put things right. It is the object of the verb 'they did,' so together the phrase means 'and did righteous deeds.'
5.grammar: 'al-' is 'the.' The word is a definite sound feminine plural ('the righteous deeds'). A sound feminine plural takes '-ātu' for the nominative (subject) but '-āti' for everything else — that single '-āti' ending serves BOTH the accusative (object) and the genitive. Here the word is the object of 'they did,' so it carries this oblique '-āti' ('-ti' on the segment shown). The plural form shows it means many good actions, a whole life of them.
5.root: ص-ل-ح (ṣ-l-ḥ) — to be sound, good, righteous, to set right

6.meaning: 'So for them' / 'then theirs is' — introduces the reward that belongs to those believers as a result. It links cause (faith and good deeds) to consequence (the reward).
6.grammar: Three pieces joined together. 'fa-' means 'so / then,' drawing the conclusion from what preceded. 'la-' means 'for / belonging to,' showing ownership. 'hum' is the attached pronoun 'them.' Put together: 'so theirs is…,' setting up the reward in the next word as something that is rightfully theirs.

7.meaning: 'A reward' — a wage or recompense earned, the compensation due to them for their faith and deeds.
7.grammar: The '-un' ending (the two-dot 'tanwīn') does two jobs: it marks the word as indefinite ('a reward,' not 'the reward'), and it is the subject/nominative ending, since this reward is the thing that 'is theirs.' Being indefinite here hints at greatness — 'a reward [of a remarkable kind].'

8.meaning: 'Other than' / 'not' — used here to negate the quality that follows: the reward is 'other than cut-off,' i.e. NOT interrupted. It functions to deny the next word's meaning.
8.grammar: A noun meaning 'other than,' commonly used to negate a following description. The '-u' (nominative) ending makes it agree with 'reward' as its describer, so it reads 'a reward [that is] other than…' Whatever comes next is thereby denied of the reward.

9.meaning: 'Cut off / diminished / ending' — something that is severed, reduced, or comes to a stop. Paired with the previous word ('other than cut-off'), it describes the reward as never-ending, unbroken, and never lessened — a favour without reproach.
9.grammar: A passive participle ('having been cut off / lessened') from the pattern 'maC-CūC.' The '-in' ending (the lower-position 'tanwīn') is genitive, because it follows and is governed by 'ghayru' ('other than ___'). So the literal reading is 'other than-[anything]-cut-off' — that is, a reward that is endless and never reduced.
9.root: م-ن-ن (m-n-n) — to cut off, diminish; also to bestow favour

1.meaning: An opening that ties this verse to what came before and poses a challenge: 'So then, what is it that...' It introduces a rhetorical question — not asking for information, but confronting the listener so that, after all the evidence of the preceding oaths, no excuse for denial remains.

parts.en: so / then (connecting to what came before)

1.grammar: Two pieces joined together. The prefix fa- is a connector meaning 'so' or 'then,' linking this verse to the truths just sworn to. mā here is an interrogative, 'what,' used as a rhetorical challenge — the sense is 'what then could possibly make you...'. There is no case ending to explain; mā is an indeclinable particle that keeps one fixed form.

2.meaning: 'Causes you to treat as a lie / drives you to reject.' The verb means to brand something false, to cry lies against it. With the attached 'you,' it asks what could be pushing the listener to dismiss the coming Judgment as a falsehood.

parts.en: to call a lie, accuse of falsehood (intensive form II)

2.grammar: The yu- prefix marks a present/ongoing action with a 'he/it' subject — the unstated subject is the 'what' of the previous word ('what makes...'). The doubled middle letter (form II, kadhdhaba) intensifies the bare root 'to lie' into 'to actively declare false, repeatedly reject.' The ending -ka is an attached object pronoun, 'you' (addressed to one man), so the whole reads 'it makes you deny.' The verb's own final vowel is -u (yukadhdhibu), the form used when nothing puts it in another state.

3.meaning: 'After this' — i.e., after all the proofs and signs already laid out. It points back to the evidence of man's noble creation and the sacred oaths, marking the denial as inexcusable now that so much has been shown.
3.grammar: An adverb of time, 'after.' Normally such a word would link to a following noun ('after X'), but here that noun is dropped because it is understood from context ('after [this evidence]'). When the noun it would attach to is omitted like this, the word is locked onto a final -u (baʿdu) — a fixed ending signalling 'the thing it refers to is already known and left unsaid.'

4.meaning: 'In / about the Recompense.' Al-dīn here is not 'religion' in the ordinary sense but the Day of Judgment and divine requital — the final reckoning when every soul is repaid for its deeds. The verse asks what makes one deny this certain accounting.

parts.en: the Judgment / Recompense, the final reckoning

4.grammar: Three pieces. The prefix bi- means 'in' or 'with respect to,' attaching the verb 'deny' to its object ('deny [with regard to] the Judgment'). al- is 'the,' making it specific and well-known. Because bi- always forces what follows into the genitive state, the noun takes the -i ending (al-dīni); the 'l' of al- assimilates into the 'd,' which is why it is pronounced and written with a doubled d (ad-dīn).

1.meaning: A rhetorical question, 'Is not...?', that expects and presses for the answer 'Yes, certainly.' It joins two pieces: the question-marker 'a- ('is it the case that?') and laysa, the verb meaning 'is not / there is not.' Together they ask 'Is it not so that...?' — a gentle but forceful way of affirming what follows: 'Surely Allah is...'

parts.en: is it the case that...? (question marker)

1.grammar: Two elements fused. The opening 'a- is the interrogative ('hamzat al-istifham') that turns the sentence into a question; here it is rhetorical, steering you toward 'yes.' Laysa is a special negating verb meaning 'is not'; it is frozen in the 3rd-person masculine singular form (ending in -a), so it points to 'He/it is not.' Question + negation together yield the affirming sense 'Is it not indeed...?'

2.meaning: Allah — the proper name of the One God, the sole Creator and Sustainer worshipped in Islam. It is not a common noun like 'a god'; it is the unique personal name of the Divine, with no plural and no gender, here standing as the subject of the sentence: the One being declared the supreme Judge.

parts.en: the (definite article, fused into the name)

2.grammar: The final -u ending is the nominative case, marking this word as the subject of the sentence (the One about whom something is being said — 'Allah... is the most just'). The leading alif here is a connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl), so it carries no vowel of its own. Although the name contains the article al- historically, it functions as a single proper name, 'Allah.'
2.root: — (proper name of Allah; no triliteral root)

3.meaning: 'By far the most just/wise in judgement' — describing Allah as the One who judges more soundly, fairly, and decisively than anyone else. The little word 'bi-' ('with/by') is attached because the verb laysa often links to its description through this particle; it does not add 'with' to the English here but simply hooks the description onto 'Allah.' The core word aḥkam is the superlative 'most just/most wise in ruling.'

parts.en: linking particle (left untranslated here; attaches the description to 'Allah')

3.grammar: Aḥkam is a superlative built on the pattern 'af'al ('most ...'), so it means 'the most just/wise judge.' It would normally end in -u, but because the particle bi- is attached, the word takes the genitive -i ending (bi-aḥkami): prepositions like bi- pull the following noun into the genitive. So the -i here is simply the case forced by bi-, and aḥkam links forward to 'the judges' ('the most just OF the judges').
3.root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m) — to judge, rule, decide with wisdom

4.meaning: 'of the judges' — i.e., of all those who pass judgement or hold authority to rule. Paired with the previous word it forms the phrase 'the most just of (all) judges,' setting Allah above every other arbiter or ruler. The word is plural, embracing the whole class of judges.
4.grammar: Ḥākim is an active participle, 'one who judges' (a judge); the prefix al- makes it definite ('the judges'). The ending -īna is the sound masculine plural in its genitive/accusative form (the kasra on the stem's final letter belongs with the case-marked stem, and -īna is the suffix). It is genitive here because the word completes the superlative phrase — 'the most just OF the judges' — the standard construction where 'most ... of [a group]' puts that group in the genitive.
4.root: ح-ك-م (ḥ-k-m) — to judge, rule, decide with wisdom
